While a client focuses on recovery, our team can build the case around it, including hiring qualified medical experts and accident reconstructionists, interviewing witnesses, collecting records and documentation, and handling the legal paperwork a spinal cord injury case may require.
What Is a Spinal Cord Injury?

A spinal cord injury occurs when damage to the spinal cord disrupts the signals that travel between the brain and the body, affecting movement, sensation, and functions like breathing and bladder control. According to
MedlinePlus

, this damage can be partial or complete, and the type of spinal cord injury a person has depends on where on the spine the injury occurs. A complete injury eliminates feeling and movement below the injury site, while an incomplete injury leaves some function intact.
Types of Spinal Cord Injuries
A
spinal cord injury
generally falls into one of the following categories, based on severity and location:
Complete Injury:
Eliminates all feeling and movement below the injury site.
Incomplete Injury:
Leaves some feeling or movement intact below the injury site.
Cervical Injury:
Damage at the neck that often causes tetraplegia, affecting the arms, legs, and torso.
Thoracic or Lumbar Injury:
Damage to the mid or lower back that generally affects the legs, a pattern known as paraplegia.
The classification of a spinal cord injury can shape the type of medical care, long-term support, and compensation a case may involve.
How Are Spine Injuries Treated?

The first few minutes after an accident can determine how much function a person keeps, since improper movement can turn an incomplete injury into a complete one. Emergency responders typically immobilize the neck and spine right away for this reason, and according to
Johns Hopkins Medicine
, treatment then focuses on stabilizing the spine, reducing swelling, and, in some cases, performing surgery to help repair the spinal cord.

Because no treatment can reverse spinal cord damage once it occurs, physical therapy, occupational therapy, and rehabilitation often become central to improving quality of life afterward. Researchers continue to develop new treatments, including modern prosthetics and electrical stimulation devices, though these remain experimental.
What to Do if You Suffered a Spinal Cord Injury
The steps taken after an accident can affect both recovery and a future claim:
Stay Still:
Back pain, numbness, tingling, or an inability to move certain limbs are signs to stop moving immediately, especially the head and neck.
Call 911:
Getting immediate medical help allows paramedics to safely immobilize the neck and spine before transport.
Get a Full Evaluation:
MRIs and other tests at the hospital can confirm whether a spine injury is present and how severe it is.
Follow the Treatment Plan:
Attending all follow-up appointments can support recovery and strengthen the medical record of the injury.
Keep Records:
Saving medical bills and documenting the recovery process can help support a claim later on.
Consult a Spinal Cord Injury Lawyer:
Legal guidance can help protect the compensation a case may be worth.
Each step builds on the last, creating a stronger foundation for both physical recovery and any claim that follows.
Spinal Disk Injuries

Spinal disks are the soft, flexible cushions between each vertebra of the spine, allowing it to move and bend without discomfort. Each disk has a tougher exterior surrounding a softer, gel-like center, and an injury can cause it to rupture, leak, herniate, or slip out of place, often placing pressure on the surrounding nerves.

That pressure can lead to chronic pain, numbness, or tingling that ranges from mild to debilitating, along with reduced mobility as the spine loses some of its natural cushioning. Muscle or tendon strain around the area can also develop as the body adjusts to the damaged disk. In most cases, spinal disk injuries can be treated, though recovery often depends on how severe the damage is.

Most of these accidents stem from someone else’s carelessness or negligence, meaning a failure to use reasonable care. When that is the case, a spinal cord injury survivor may be entitled to financial compensation from the at-fault party.
Long-Term Effects of Spinal Cord Injuries
Understanding how an injury occurred is just one aspect of the situation. What follows can shape the rest of a person’s life. According to the
National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke
, a spinal cord injury often brings lasting consequences that extend well beyond the initial diagnosis, including:
Permanent paralysis or chronic pain requiring lifelong adaptive equipment and care
Secondary medical complications like respiratory problems and pressure sores
A loss of independence in work, driving, or daily tasks
Financial strain from equipment, home modifications, and long-term care
Emotional impact on relationships and mental well-being

How Do You Prove a Spinal Cord Injury Claim?
Because the consequences run this deep, a claim strong enough to cover them takes careful preparation from the start. Proving a spinal cord injury claim requires establishing several key elements:
Duty and Breach:
Showing that another party owed a duty of care and failed to meet that standard through negligence.
Causation:
Connecting that negligence directly to the accident and the resulting spinal cord injury.
Medical Evidence:
Supporting the claim with police reports, accident reconstruction, and testimony from treating physicians.
Future Costs:
Bringing in economists and life care planners to testify about lifetime care needs and lost earning capacity, given how often these injuries require long-term treatment.
Together, these elements build the foundation for a claim that reflects the full extent of what a spinal cord injury may cost.
Who Can Be Held Liable?

Liability for a spinal cord injury generally falls on the party or parties whose negligence caused the accident. Depending on the circumstances, that responsibility can extend to more than one type of party, such as:
Drivers who cause traffic accidents through distraction, speeding, or other reckless behavior
Property owners who fail to address hazardous conditions on their premises
Employers who fail to provide adequate training, supervision, or safety measures
Manufacturers responsible for defective products or equipment
Medical providers whose errors or malpractice result in a spinal cord injury
Once negligence is established, the at-fault party becomes the defendant, and the injured party, as the plaintiff, carries the burden of proving the claim.
What Types of Damages Can I Recover in a Spinal Cord Injury Case?
With liability established, the next question is what that responsibility is worth. Colorado law allows injured people to recover several categories of damages:
Medical care, including past treatment and future needs
Equipment and home or vehicle modifications
Lost wages and reduced earning capacity
Pain and suffering
Loss of activities that once mattered to daily life
Punitive damages, in cases involving particularly reckless conduct
Our
Denver spinal cord injury lawyer
team works to pursue the full combination of damages available, reflecting both the immediate costs of an injury and the way it may continue to affect a person’s life going forward.
Time Limit for Spine Injury Cases
None of that compensation remains available once the filing deadline passes. Colorado law generally gives injured people two years from the date of an accident to file a personal injury lawsuit under
. When a spinal cord injury results from a motor vehicle accident, the deadline extends to three years under
. Missing either deadline can permanently bar recovery.

Exceptions to these deadlines may apply in certain situations, but they remain the exception rather than the rule. Because determining which deadline applies, and whether an exception might extend it, is not always straightforward, having legal guidance early on can help ensure a claim is filed on time.

faqs.question: How much is a spinal cord injury case worth?

children.text: The value of a spinal cord injury case depends on the injury’s severity, required medical care, and lost earning capacity. Cases involving permanent paralysis typically settle for more than those involving temporary impairment.

faqs.question: Can you recover compensation for paralysis after an accident?

children.text: Yes, Colorado law allows injured people to recover compensation for paralysis caused by another party’s negligence. Damages can include medical care, home modifications, lost income, and other costs associated with adjusting to a permanent disability.

faqs.question: How long does a spinal cord injury lawsuit take?

children.text: The timeline for a spinal cord injury lawsuit can vary widely, generally ranging from one to three years depending on the severity of the injury and whether the case settles or proceeds to trial.

faqs.question: What causes most spinal cord injuries?

children.text: Motor vehicle accidents cause most spinal cord injuries in Colorado, followed by falls, acts of violence, and sports or recreational accidents.

faqs.question: What if my spinal cord injury symptoms appear later?

children.text: Some spinal cord injury symptoms do not appear until days after an accident. Seek medical attention if you notice numbness, tingling, or weakness, and consult a
Denver spinal cord injury lawyer
promptly to protect your claim.
